books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Transcendentalism

stimulus.text: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Self-Reliance," 1841: "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. Accept the place the divine providence has found for you, the society of your contemporaries, the connection of events."
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim quotation from Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Self-Reliance," Essays: First Series (1841). Public domain; wording checked against the published text.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Emerson's essay most directly challenged which of the following?

options.text: Imitating European thought and conforming to custom
The growth of canals and railroads
options.misconception: Canals and railroads were the big changes of the 1840s, so it is easy to tie any protest to them.
Emerson wrote in the age of Jackson, so it is easy to make the essay about Jackson.

options.text: The spread of the Second Great Awakening
options.misconception: Revival meetings were everywhere in these years, so it is easy to make the essay answer them.

rationales.A: Self-trust is the opposite of copying others; Emerson's whole essay attacks conformity and imitation.
rationales.B: The passage says nothing about canals, railroads, or transportation of any kind.
rationales.C: Emerson does not name Jackson or any election; his target is how people think, not who governs.
rationales.D: The revivals preached conversion through feeling, while Emerson preached trusting the self; they were neighbors, not his target.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what 'trust thyself' pushes against. It pushes against taking your opinions from others.
2. Widen the lens. Emerson's larger target was Americans repeating Europe and repeating each other.
Background: in 'The American Scholar' Emerson called for an end to apprenticeship to foreign learning.
Remember: to find what a writer challenges, look for the opposite of what the writer praises.
